                    [0-5802] paragraph
                      [0-3612] StaticText: Understanding the MVC pattern is key to understanding Rails. MVC divides your application into three layers: Model, View, and Controller, each with a specific responsibility.
                    [0-5803] div

                        [0-5810] strong
                          [0-3615] StaticText: Model layer
                      [0-3616] StaticText: represents the domain model (such as Account, Product, Person, Post, etc.) and encapsulates the business logic specific to your application. In Rails, database-backed model classes are derived from
                      [0-5811] code
                        [0-3617] StaticText: ActiveRecord::Base
                      [0-3618] StaticText: .
                      [0-5812] link: Active Record
                      [0-3620] StaticText: allows you to present the data from database rows as objects and embellish these data objects with business logic methods. Although most Rails models are backed by a database, models can also be ordinary Ruby classes, or Ruby classes that implement a set of interfaces as provided by the
                      [0-5813] link: Active Model
                      [0-3622] StaticText: module.
                    [0-5814] div
                      [0-5815] heading: View layer
                      [0-5816] link: Permalink: View layer
                    [0-5819] paragraph
                      [0-3624] StaticText: The
                      [0-5820] emphasis
                        [0-5821] strong
                          [0-3625] StaticText: View layer
                      [0-3626] StaticText: is composed of "templates" that are responsible for providing appropriate representations of your application's resources. Templates can come in a variety of formats, but most view templates are HTML with embedded Ruby code (ERB files).                       [0-3771] link: Action View

                          [0-3631] StaticText: Controller layer
                      [0-3632] StaticText: is responsible for handling incoming HTTP requests and providing a suitable response. Usually, this means returning HTML, but Rails controllers can also generate XML, JSON, PDFs, mobile-specific views, and more. Controllers load and manipulate models, and render view templates in order to generate the appropriate HTTP response.
